opus-5.5.text:
I think it shapes the culture quite a lot, mostly in terms of psychological safety. At many companies with forced ranking, where the bottom few percent are let go every year, people end up competing with the colleague sitting next to them. You become cautious about sharing ideas, you avoid risky projects, and you optimize for looking good in the review cycle rather than for doing the most important work.

At Nvidia, at least from my perspective in research, that pressure isn't really there. Jensen has talked about this: he would rather invest in people and help them improve than churn through them. The result is that people are more willing to collaborate across teams. If I'm working on generative models for physical AI and I need help from the systems people or the graphics people, they're willing to jump in, because helping me doesn't cost them anything in some zero-sum ranking.

It also lets people take long bets. A lot of what Nvidia is known for today, CUDA, the early deep learning work, even some of the world-model and simulation research we do, looked like it might not pay off for years. If you're worried about being in the bottom ten percent this year, you don't sign up for a project that might take five years to matter. Without that fear, people are more comfortable working on things that are ambitious and uncertain.

That said, it doesn't mean there's no accountability. The bar is high, and the intensity is high. Jensen is very direct, and feedback often happens in the open rather than being saved for an annual review. So instead of a ranking system, the pressure comes from the mission and from your peers. People want to do great work because the problems are exciting and everyone around them is pushing hard. I think that's a healthier kind of pressure, and it's one reason people tend to stay at Nvidia for a long time.

r001.rationale: The response says forced-ranking employees become cautious about sharing ideas, then contrasts Nvidia’s lack of that pressure and describes greater willingness to collaborate. This communicates that reduced fear supports openness.

r002.rationale: It says employees are not competing with nearby colleagues in a zero-sum ranking and that helping another person does not cost them anything, reducing pressure to stand out at colleagues’ expense.

r003.rationale: It describes forced ranking as making employees compete with colleagues and avoid sharing ideas, then links the absence of that zero-sum pressure to greater collaboration.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it has a very deep effect, and it's one of the things that made me stay at Nvidia for so long. When you know the company isn't going to cut the bottom five or ten percent every year just to hit a number, people stop playing defense. You don't spend your energy making sure you look better than the person next to you. You spend it on the problem.

In a lot of research organizations, the stack ranking creates a kind of quiet politics. People hoard information, they're careful about who they collaborate with, they pick safe projects because a failed project could put them at the bottom. At Nvidia, I've seen the opposite. Someone on my team can take on something that might not work for two years, and nobody is calculating whether that puts their job at risk. That's how you get things like the early generative models or the simulation work. Those were not obvious bets when we started.

I also think Jensen's view is that if someone is struggling, that's often a management problem first. Maybe they're in the wrong role, maybe they weren't given the right context. So the instinct is to move people, coach them, give them another shot, rather than exit them. Jensen has said something like he would rather torture you into greatness than let you go, and that's half a joke, but it's also true. The bar is very high. It's not a comfortable place. But the discomfort comes from the standards, not from fear of being eliminated.

The other consequence is loyalty and institutional memory. People stay ten, fifteen, twenty years. When you're working on something as complicated as a full-stack AI platform, having people who remember why a decision was made eight years ago is incredibly valuable. You can't build that if you're churning the bottom of the organization every cycle.

So to me it's not a soft policy. It's a very deliberate choice about what kind of behavior you want to incentivize, and I think it's a big part of why the culture feels like one team rather than a tournament.

r001.rationale: The response says employees feel less fear of losing their jobs and take more risks, but it does not state that they are more willing to express views they would otherwise withhold.

r002.rationale: It says employees stop spending energy trying to look better than the person next to them, reducing pressure to stand out aggressively.

r003.rationale: It describes stack ranking as creating politics, information hoarding, and caution about collaboration, linking competition to harder collaboration.

astra-6.text:
I think it gives people more room to take risks and learn. If you’re constantly worried about being ranked at the bottom, you may choose safer projects or focus on looking better than your colleagues. That can make collaboration harder, especially in research, where a good idea might take a long time to work.

When the emphasis is on helping people improve, you have more reason to share what you know, ask for help, and be honest when something isn’t working. You still need high expectations and clear feedback. But you can hold people accountable while giving them the support and time to succeed. I think that combination is very valuable for an innovative company.

r001.rationale: The response says employees can take risks, share knowledge, ask for help, and be honest, but it does not connect job security to expressing views they would otherwise withhold out of fear of dismissal.

r002.rationale: It says fear of being ranked at the bottom can lead employees to focus on looking better than colleagues, and links avoiding bottom-ranked elimination with more room to take risks and learn.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says that focusing on looking better than colleagues can make collaboration harder.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it gives people more confidence to collaborate and take risks. If you know that someone has to end up at the bottom and leave, you may start competing with your teammates instead of helping them. When that pressure is removed, it’s easier to share ideas, admit mistakes, and ask for help.

That doesn’t mean performance doesn’t matter. You still need high expectations and honest feedback. But the emphasis becomes, “How can we help this person succeed?” That’s especially valuable in research, where a good idea can take time and several failed attempts to develop.

r001.rationale: It links the removal of the pressure that someone must leave with greater willingness to share ideas, admit mistakes, and ask for help.

r002.rationale: It says employees might compete with teammates, but does not clearly state that avoiding bottom-tier elimination reduces pressure to aggressively stand out from colleagues.

r003.rationale: It says employees may compete with teammates instead of helping them, clearly connecting competition with reduced collaboration.
